title: 3.48 Million Australian Dollars Report Polished by ChatGPT: Australia's Social Media Ban Technology Basis Faced Backfire from Fake Citations

content_html:
Australia spent 3.48 million Australian dollars to commission an age verification technology test, but ended up in an embarrassing situation due to a report that had been watered down with AI. The British organization ACCS, which conducted the test, initially denied using artificial intelligence, but later admitted to using AI to rewrite parts of the report after The Guardian discovered ChatGPT metadata in the report link.

Fake citations come to light

This key report, which paved the way for a social media ban for Australians under 16, was based on real technical tests. However, the references in the "emerging technologies" section were full of errors. The Guardian found that there were six incorrect references in the same section: some DOIs pointed to non-existent papers, others linked to wrong documents, and the combination of authors, journals, and years did not match any known research. Even more absurdly, the "correction list" submitted by ACCS later also had problems with incorrect years and authors. One of the papers' main authors clearly stated that they had never participated in this study, and the paper was published after the time they claimed to have accessed it.

Government trust further damaged

ACCS insisted that AI was only used to make the language more concise and that the links themselves were correct, so it wasn't an issue. However, the government contractor has a history of using AI to water down reports. Last year, Deloitte returned 440,000 Australian dollars in contract payments due to AI hallucination errors, and the Australian federal government already has a negative attitude toward such behavior. The academic community warned that false citations, regardless of whether they were caused by AI or not, could mislead government decisions and erode public trust. Some lawmakers have already demanded that the contractors apologize and refund the money. The excuse that only 26 pages of a thousand-page report involved citations and revealed "a few errors" is unlikely to ease this trust crisis surrounding AI ghostwriting.

content_html_zh:
澳大利亚花费348万澳元委托进行年龄验证技术测试，却因一份被AI淡化的报告而陷入尴尬境地。 进行测试的英国组织 ACCS 最初否认使用人工智能，但在《卫报》发现报告链接中的 ChatGPT 元数据后，承认使用人工智能重写了报告的部分内容。

虚假引文曝光

这份重要报告基于真实的技术测试，为 16 岁以下澳大利亚人禁止使用社交媒体铺平了道路。 然而，“新兴技术”部分的参考资料却充满了错误。 《卫报》发现同一部分中有 6 个错误的参考文献：一些 DOI 指向不存在的论文，另一些则链接到错误的文档，而且作者、期刊和年份的组合与任何已知的研究都不匹配。 更荒唐的是，ACCS后来提交的“更正清单”也存在年份和作者不正确的问题。 其中一位论文的主要作者明确表示，他们从未参与过这项研究，并且该论文是在他们声称访问过该研究的时间之后发表的。

政府信任进一步受损

ACCS 坚称人工智能只是为了让语言更加简洁，而且链接本身是正确的，所以这不是问题。 然而，政府承包商有使用人工智能淡化报告的历史。 去年，德勤因人工智能幻觉错误，退回了44万澳元的合同付款，澳大利亚联邦政府对此类行为已经持否定态度。 学术界警告说，虚假引用，无论是否由人工智能造成，都可能误导政府决策并削弱公众信任。 一些立法者已经要求承包商道歉并退还资金。 千页报告中只有 26 页涉及引用并披露了“一些错误”的借口不太可能缓解围绕人工智能代写的信任危机。
